title: Block 1 Assignment  Submit One Mini-Design Challenge (Final)
pageTexts: Block 1 Assignment: Submit One Mini-Design Challenge (Final) Process Document 1. Context and learners: Who is it for, and what learning need does it address? This project is design for middle school teachers and students taking part in a a PBL-style project called Our Golden Record. The project is based on the Golden Record project that was part of NASA's Voyager missions in the 1970s. The goal is for student groups to crate a modern version of this, utilizing modern media to represent their own communities. The AI Council is available to students at various points of the project and simulates an advisory group or board. It gives teachers a tool for students to learn how consulting with such as group can improve their work, gaining valuable perspectives they not otherwise get. While teachers may arrange for in-person guest speakers, field trips, and connection to actual experts, the AI Council can fill in knowledge gaps and give students practice at using a AI-enabled tool. 2. Design goals: What were you trying to achieve (learning outcomes and/or experience goals)? Learning goals for students: Evaluate what defines your "community" by creating and selecting material that will be communicated. Produce a range of media that communicates complex human concepts to an unfamiliar audience Apply mathematical modeling to manage project specifications and constraints Conduct sustained research into your community to present a multidisciplinary and multimodal digital artifact. Demonstrate effective teamwork and project management skill in project groups to meet a launch deadline. My personal goal for the project was to create a flexible for teachers that adds value to such a project, and is not AI/tech for the sake of AI/tech. 3. Key design decisions: What did you choose and why (e.g., scaffolds, feedback strategy, council roles and handoffs, modality choices)? What learning theories did you

apply and/or integrate into your design? I scaffolded the release of the AI council members to align with different project phases. In practice, teachers would regulate student access to the AI council to particular times, such as one time during and at the conclusion of each project phases. This would include handoffs from the students to the council members, and can even include back and forth between council members. I gave each council member prompting to be reflective; they do not merely provide answers, or even direct guidance, but ask open-ended follow-up questions that spur critical thinking and help students expand the scope of their research or presentations. 4. Learner interaction flow: How does a learner use this? What inputs do they provide and what do they get back? Learners can provide either specific questions in a prompt box (eg. "How can we involve local indigenous history in our project?") or they can upload artifacts for the council to analyze and comment on, such as their Community Charter or their preliminary artifact list. They receive responses back from members, either one at a time, or at the same time. I have built-in accessibility features coded into my UI to address the age and grade-level of the students (aimed at 6-7th graders), including: larger font size for readability on screens, high-contract for text and background, text output is throttled to approximately 175 wpm with pauses at the end of each sentence, spacing between paragraphs and questions, directions to aim for grade 6 lexile level for all output, including safeguards for language and content. 5. Iteration evidence: What feedback did you receive and what changed as a result? I received feedback to consider interactions between council members. I have added a Send Response To... button after a user gets a response from a council member. This simulates interaction between the council. On the back-end I included an instruction for the receiving council member to analyze the response critically and provide either an alternate idea or one critique of the original response. Feedback has also motivated be to turn this into an AI Council template for teacher's to create custom personas and enter in their own project information. 6. Limitations and next steps: What’s not working yet, what assumptions are you making, and what would you improve next iteration? The interaction between council member has mixed results, and sometimes council members have stock answers that fall back to their original prompting. They also

sometimes refer to what should be teacher-facing information or prompts (specific standards or pedagogical language). I would address this by editing the council prompts further, and giving overall guidance to avoid such terms or topics. I would also like to provide more student-facing information on the landing page, including project phase details, learning goals, or suggested prompts, without scaffolding too much. I also want to add reminders of the expertise of each council member, with overlays/bios or tooltips. I also need to test with some project examples, either created by me or with another generative tool, such as NotebookLM. 7. Generative AI attribution: Tools used and a brief description of how they contributed? To build my council, I created five separate personae on Google Gems that use Google Gemini. To create a simple UI, I used Cursor to build a web interface that puts each Gem on one screen with a prompt input. Because Gems cannot yet be embedded directly, or have multi-Gem capability on the same screen, the Gem's instructions are pasted into my web app's code, along with a Gemini API that uses Gemini Flash 2.5. As a result, the responses from the members are not as consistent and high quality as asking the Gems directly in the Google interface. To help with this, I added more detail into the context of the web app for each persona. This made up for some of the context that the Gems had within the Google interface (on Google platform, the Gems have access to a NotebookLM notebook I have that contains project documents and conversations about project planning). The web UI is hosted on a simple web app server I use for other projects, called Vercel and is backed up on a Github repository.

title: Block 1 Reflection Submission
pageTexts: Step 1: Looking Back — What You Learned To start, let's focus on your key takeaways from the first five weeks. What are 2–3 of your most significant takeaways from Block 1? Was there a specific concept (like ZPD, Experiential Learning, or Bloom’s Taxonomy), a reading, or a class moment that genuinely shifted how you think about AI and learning? What surprised you most—either about the AI tools we explored or about yourself as a learner? Feel free to jot down your thoughts on these points, and then we'll move on to the next step! You said One significant takeaway is there is a balance with using emerging technology for learning; while this tech can provide ample opportunities for students to engage with new learning, concepts, and each other, there is a risk that these tools, such as chatbots, LLMs, etc. do TOO much for the learner. Now, let’s go a bit deeper into how this tension plays out in reality. Choose ONE of the following options to explore further: Option A: What Worked – Think about a specific moment in Block 1— perhaps a hands-on lab or a prototype—where you felt the AI hit the "sweet spot." What made it work as a partner rather than a replacement? Option B: What Was Challenging – Was there a moment where you felt that "authorship slip away" while using a tool? What did that tell you about your own assumptions or the limits of that technology? Option C: Connecting to Your Context – In your specific professional role, how do you see yourself navigating this balance? What would it look like to implement these tools while ensuring students remain the primary "sense- makers"? Which of these resonates most with you right now? You said Option A: In my AI Council activity, I made some intentional design choices to make sure the learners was not over or under-scaffolded. I prompted the council chatbots to provide their output in the form or guided or reflective questions, as opposed to direct answers.

I adjusted the output of the council to be limited to be a certain number of words/tokens, and to push learners to seek out additional resources, such as primary research sources (museums, universities, non-profits, etc) to encourage first-hand learning experiences in real life. While the chatbots can provide guidance, they leave major decisions up to the learners. I also provided some accessibility guidelines on the council platform including: larger, high-contrast fonts, larger line spacing with line breaks between paragraphs or questions, guidance to limit the Lexile level of output to Grade 6 (this was a middle school PBL project), and throttling the output so it displays slower and pauses at the end of each sentence to reduce cognitive load and allow time for comprehension and reflection. Now, let’s wrap up this reflection by looking at the road ahead. As you move into Block 2 (which focuses on VR/AR/XR and Immersive Learning), what question or tension from Block 1 are you carrying with you? What's one thing you want to do differently—in your practice, your mindset, or your engagement with the course—as we pivot toward spatial and embodied learning? Is there anything from the "AI in Learning" block you feel you want to revisit or go deeper on later? Branching Choice: Would you like to continue on this final step of the reflection, switch to a specific question about Block 2, or finish the reflection for now? You said I would like to keep my "hybrid" approach in mind for Block 2, more specifically how to use emerging tech as an additive tool that brings something to the learner that they could not have otherwise. I am not a supporter of tech for the sake of tech when it comes to education. So with immersive tech, if it does add value, I also want it to be in moderation and still encourage students to interact with each other and the world around them, whenever possible.

title: Block 2 Reflection Submission
pageTexts: Block 2 Reflection Submission Reflecting on your experience with wicked problems , immersive affordances , and the cross-disciplinary collaboration : What are 2–3 of your most significant takeaways from Block 2? Was there a specific moment—perhaps during team building, prototyping, or the final showcase—that shifted how you think about immersive learning or learning design? What surprised you most about the content, the collaboration, the platform you used, or even yourself as a designer? Take a moment to share your thoughts on these, and we'll move to the design and practice dimension next! One significant takeaway was how immersive spaces can be used for engaging learning in and out of the modern classroom. Although they can be challenging technically, when done well they can provide memorable experiential learning. Another takeaway is how meaningful cross-disciplinary projects can be. It was a great experience to collaboratively plan the museum project with the MUSE classmates and learn how to manage the project between the two courses. o help us flesh out this part of your reflection, could you share: 1. Which of these areas (the collaboration, the platform, or the "wicked" nature of the problem) felt the most difficult or uncomfortable for you? 2. How did you handle it? Did you find a creative workaround, or is it a design tension you are still sitting with as the block ends? 3. What does this reveal about your current assumptions or your professional practice? Would you like to: Continue reflecting on this challenge? Switch to a different Option (A or C) for Step 2? Move on to Step 3: Looking Forward? 1. There were some points of challenge during the project on the topic as well as the logistics of the project. One issue was focusing the wicked problem of water resource use, which is a sprawling subject with many facets. It was a challenge to figure out where and how to focus it, then how to bring that focus to the exhibit. A result was somewhat of an unfocused exhibit that had parts that felt disjointed. Related to this challenge were the

technical design challenges of the platform. It was a struggle to get our ideas off the page and into practical use on the Spatial platform. The learning curve was steep with UI that did not feel intuitive or easy to pick up. As a result, our exhibit was not as interactive or immersive as we would have hoped. 2. We did focus in on three aspects of the issue, using our learning objectives as guidance. I don't think we fully achieved a cohesive experience, but we were able to create an exhibit that was visually clean and limited cognitive overload. Some of the technical issues we were not able to overcome, such as creating more interaction and reflection, embedding media, or adding to the physical layout of the space. 3. I think it's important to have realistic expectations and goals for this type of work, especially with time constraints. I also realized the importance of project and process management for a group of collaborators. For such a project, having enough time to experiment with the tools is critical, which also allows for more creative designing and iteration. I often work alone so it was a solid reminder about the importance of establishing norms and processes for collaboration, taking all members' needs and personal goals in mind. To wrap up your Block 2 reflection (aiming for 100–150 words): As you move into Block 3 (Learning Systems and Experiences) , what question or tension from this immersive project are you carrying with you? What is one thing you want to do differently —in your practice, your mindset, or how you engage with your team—as the course progresses? Is there anything from the "Digital Museum" block that you want to revisit or go deeper on later? Would you like to continue with this final step, switch to a different reflection topic, or finish for now? One thing I will carry with me is how to balance collaboration with individual creativity and motivation in a cross-disciplinary project or a project with multiple stakeholders. In my personal work, I develop edTech tools and apps for teachers and students. I often need to balance my own expertise or opinions with how something should look or be built, with the constraints a teacher or student may have. I want to make sure I am taking the time to research, engineer, plan, and iterate in order to develop products that are efficacious, engaging, and fun, as well as useful for the most number of people in my target audience.

title: DGMD E57 - Digital Museum Prototype  Design + Process Document
pageTexts: DGMD E57 - Digital Museum Prototype: Design + Process Document Bob Kelly Design Rationale Learning goals were developed after drafting and refining the core messages for the project. The two messages that we settled on were (1) water is a precious resource, and (2) humans have solved and can solve problems related to local water issues, using technology. The learning goals were developed with the core audience of Grade 6-12 students in mind. The four learning objectives that we developed were: Learners identify historical uses of water by humans. Learners examine artifacts to relate historical water use to technological solutions. Learners use interactive models to reflect on their own water use. Learners connect solutions to water use problems to issues in their local community. Given constraints of time and technology, we were able to focus more on some of the objectives than others, but the intent was to connect visitors to historical and contemporary water use and learn how innovative technology can help solve the ‘wicked problem’ of water resource management and scarcity. We designed a circular spatial layout to encourage open exploration of ideas and all call to mind the concept of the water cycle and how technologies are adapted through time, from ancient to modern contexts. We grouped artifacts and presentations into three main areas focusing on irrigation, transportation, and filtration and designed a central meeting/ classroom area to accommodate groups such as school class visits, or virtual presentations. We planned an interactive reflection wall (not fully prototyped) as a way for visitors to reflect on their experience in the exhibit and connect the issue to their lives and their communities. We placed 3D artifacts and image-and-text pairings along the walls of the circular space with an infographic on the floor to ground visitors to the issue of global water use. The planned “Where do you get your water?” wall, while not yet interactive, anchors visitors to our fourth learning objective to connect them to local water issues in their community. This reflection zone is our main transfer mechanism, as it gently pushes visitors to shift from learning about distant case studies to considering the sources and infrastructures that make their own water use possible.

Learning Science Integration We used backward design by thinking about the big ideas we wanted visitors to take away from the exhibit and designing learning objectives around those ideas. Although there are not assessments in the experience per se, we thought about how to encourage visitors to self-reflect on their relationship to water within their communities. We then thought about the activities and content that could help visitors meet those objects, but using multimodal artifacts, reflective questions, and an intentionally designed space to encourage discussion and questioning. As our primary audience is 6-12th graders, we adapted text passages to be age- and grade- level appropriate, adjusting vocabulary, volume of text, and complexity of language to limit cognitive overload. The 3D objects were designed to promote deep processing by making abstract ideas like changes in filtration technology physically present in the space. Finally, the water reflection wall and benches are meant to ground all the water concepts learned in the user’s personal experience. Prompts such as “Where do you get your water?” ask visitors to connect exhibit content to their own homes and communities, which is critical for transfer beyond the museum. Our original plan was to engineer an interactive post-it wall that creates a sea of responses to this question, so exhibit viewers can see the scale of how water affects everyone around them. Individual Contribution As a current and former teacher and curriculum developer, I took the lead on turning our initial conversation about core messages and big ideas into four learning objectives. I tried to keep the number of objectives between 3-5, and use student and teacher-friendly language. I focused on achievable objectives but did not necessarily consider time or technology constraints, as the objectives were developed at the start of the project. I used action verbs that addressed various levels of complexity and Bloom’s Taxonomy, and avoided general terms such as “understand” and “know.” I contributed to all of the group’s weekly planning meetings and discussion and focused on the design of the space and editing and placement of assets within Spatial. I took an image from the MUSE group members that was a mock-up for the exhibit and turned it into a 3D object using meshy.ai . I then worked through several ideas and prototypes for the layout of the exhibit, gallery walls, and seating, collaborating with the group throughout. I troubleshooted and continuously updated the Spatial space as we neared project deadlines and received feedback. Interaction and Reflection

We iterated on several ideas in the early phases of the project, collaborating with the MUSE team members. When they sent a prototype idea for the museum layout, I built several versions of a 3D model for the exhibit walls and presented them to the group for feedback. The MUSE members selected the model they liked best and that was aligned with their vision and the objectives of the exhibit. As our class members handled some of the technical aspects of the project, the MUSE members presented ideas that we tested and tried to determine if they were feasible, while contributing our own content ideas. During in-class group work we received some helpful advice and feedback from Luis and Andy on some of the technical aspects of the project, such as Unity integration and meshy troubleshooting. After our presentation, we received a lot of helpful feedback about the visitor experience, layout of the exhibit such as wayfinding and keeping visitors focused, and how to more authentically connect the visitors’ experience to self-reflection. We were able to integrate a few small changes so far, such as adding a welcome screen and wayfinding, helping visitors to the exhibit when arriving in Spatial. A roof was also added to the exhibit to focus visitors’ attention and experience more. Collaboration Reflection Overall the collaboration worked well with few roadblocks. We established norms over email and decided on Google Spaces to collaborate and do weekly calls for planning and progress updates. One challenge we found was the difference in project deadlines for the two classes. Although both deadlines felt relatively aggressive, the MUSE class’ deadline was prior to ours, so it led to some stress and rushed changes or decisions that may have sacrificed quality in some aspects of the project. We also had some technical problems within Google that did not allow for seamless communication from the start. I would choose a different comms platform, such as Slack, next time for better collaboration. I would also have liked to add more to our physical space in terms of variety of interactions for the user. Because of the way we delegated the work, I think it made it more challenging to bring many new ideas to the table. We instead had ideas early on and stuck within those ideas and our “roles,” without much flexibility. We also had several group members (including myself) with some personal/ work matters that did not allow for as much execution time as we would have liked.

title: DGMD E57 Mini Design Challenge III  Multimodal Creation
pageTexts: DGMD E57 Mini Design Challenge III: Multimodal Creation Mini Design Challenge III Process Document For this assignment, I expanded on Mini Design Challenge II by create a 1-page handout for students as a guide for their project. This corresponds to the objective for students to self-assess their progress toward the learning goals and the success criteria of the PBL project. Students would individually have a copy of this document, in print and/or digital form. They would use it to formatively assess their progress at each of the four project phases. It could also be used for peer assessment at the conclusion of the project. It has three main sections: 1) Learning Objectives that represent different levels of Bloom's Taxonomy and different skills. These objectives were written with cross-curricular standards in mind; 2) Assessment Criteria that students use to check their progress individually and as a group. Teachers could direct students to use it as a checklist or formulate a rating or number system (better still, students could be in charge of this system); and 3) Standards. These are pulled directly from standards documents and represent the main assessed standards for this project. There are other supporting standards that the teacher can formatively address throughout. I used the following Learning Design principles to guide the creation of this multimedia artifact: PBL/experiential learning: learners take part in a realistic project and produce an actual artifact by its end. They are given realistic constraints and criteria to follow. They participate in several rounds of self and peer assessment to guide their designs. Cognitive load: This artifact reduces cognitive load by providing a visual representation and reminder of project objective and assessment criteria. Students use the artifact to check their progress formatively, and often. Backwards design: Standards and assessments were determined before learning objectives and activities were planned. This allowed for clearer alignment between the project goals and student tasks. This document connects the learning activities (objectives) with standards and assessment. Learning in context: addressed through PBL, students develop skills and knowledge by working through a hands-on project set in a real-world scenario. This artifact keeps learners within the context of the project.

AI collaboration process: I utilized NotebookLM which contains my project files, including all standards documents, my project brief, and PBL guidance. NotebookLM allows for source-specific generation and allows for limited source generation, which can cut down on errors and hallucinations. It also keeps all of my uploaded files private and sandboxed. Using the standards documents for social studies, math, science, and ELA, and my Project Brief, I asked it to create a 1-page infographic document with some guidance (see below for my prompt). I generated an image on Standard mode at first for the first pass (assuming this uses Nano Banana but not entirely sure), then two iterations on the Detailed (beta) mode. Each iteration, I made adjustments to my prompt based on the results. Results were overall what I was hoping for, with a couple caveats. One is inconsistent spelling and grammar due to generative text mistakes. The other are accessibility issues, such as color contrasts, font consistencies and graphics that are generally too "busy." Here is how I could address these issues: Use NotebookLM for an outline of an infographic then make it manually using a design tool such as Adobe Illustrator or Figma. Use generative AI to produce individual assets, such as graphics, icons, tables, etc. Then manually create text-based assets and combine the two, again in a design tool. Use a different AI model or tool that is known to be better at generating text and addressing accessibility concerns. Similarly, I could run the generated artifact through a different image generation, using image-to-image generation to correct spelling or make other minor changes.

title: Final Emerging Technology Pitch
pageTexts: Final Emerging Technology Pitch Additional process documentation Project and Technology Overview This project was a continuation of the AI chatbot and PBL council assignments, which originally used Google Gems and Google Gemini as the basis for the human-AI interaction. At the time, it was not possible to directly embed Gems into other products or sites, so I created separate personas for my original PBL Council project, which was a middle-school interdisciplinary project that challenged groups of students to create a "Golden Record" that represents them and their community, which would be "sent" to space and potentially found by alien civilizations far in the future. I had Google AI Studio build the original bones of a website where the council would be hosted. I then connected a Google AI API to the project and gave the LLM specific global instructions (for audience, safety, tone, style, etc.), and gave more specific prompting to the custom-made personas. I uploaded the project to Github and connected it to Vercel, which I use for web-app project development, and which has cheap or free database hosting. I continued to refine the code (combination of Javascript, HTML, and CSS) and the project using Cursor Pro, which has access to a variety of coding and natural language models, primarily using ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor's in-house models, Composer and Composer 2. I tested consistently for model performance as well as for UX purposes. The next phase of the project, which I am submitting here, was to generalize the PBL council creator into its own product for teachers to use to create their own stakeholder councils. This involved creating additional hand-offs between human and AI contributions. I tweaked the format and UI many times to improve clarity, usability, and accessibility. Google Gemini Flash 2.5 and 3.1 are used to support the user's creation of the PBL council, parsing project brief documents and analyzing other user-entered information, such as project goals, learning objectives, and guiding questions. After research AI chatbot safety issues, I consulted with the KORA benchmark for AI safety and decided to swap Google Gemini as the main chatbot interface with GPT-5.2, which scored much higher on the benchmark for AI child safety than Gemini, and would still be cost- effective during testing and development. Gemini is still used in the Council Creator to parse documents, suggest project details, and find local expert council members. A defining feature of the project is its implementation of a hybrid approach to human-AI interaction. In the Council Creator, users can enter information in any of the project input

fields, including the project brief, learning objectives, project phases, milestones, and council member bios. Users can then ask the AI to fill in remaining fields with suggestions based on the topic, existing project briefs or other details, the grade level of students, and geographic area. Built into the project is the ability to search for local experts in the topic's discipline or field. After generating AI personas for the council, users can swap out AI council members for human members, either entering information manually (bio, contact info, photo), or by using the LLM to search for a relevant expert. The AI is prompted to search at local universities, community organizations, non-profits, etc. for individuals in a particular field of expertise. If an individual is not found, organizations can be selected with their contact information. For K-12 students this feature is not available on the student-side in the interactive Stakeholder Council (university students and beyond can swap out AI members for human members at any time). In addition to this 'hybrid' approach in the Council Creator, there are also features in the Stakeholder Council to promote human interaction. When users ask the council members a question or provide a prompt, AI personas are designed to provide structured guidance but not directly give students answers. Instead they answer with reflective prompts, such as "How do you think you could more clearly present the data to an audience?" or "What types of cultural groups might be left out with this approach?" Users can ask one follow- up question to a response. Also, council members will push students to interact with their group members ("Consider talking to your group about...") or resources in their community, with a "Follow-up in your community" section to the response. This feature also uses geographic location taken from a user's IP address (or approximation) to seek out local resources and contact information. Along with these technical feature, I made several guiding decisions to promote learning design best practices, accessibility and safety, especially for K-12 users, including: Increased font size in council responses, using a sans-serif font Council responses are limited to a certain number of words/tokens Council responses are displayed full-screen (or split-screen when multiple members are prompted) Council response text speed is throttled to display slower than a typical LLM, animating word-by-word and pausing after each sentence Line breaks are added between paragraphs, bullet points, and questions K-12 users are given a character maximum of 144 characters for their prompts (and will have only two uses per visit to the council)

LLM model shifted to a higher-score model from the KORA AI Child Safety benchmark (revisited often) Global prompts given to the LLM for child awareness ("You are speaking with a 6th grader. Explain topics simply when possible.") and blocks of prompting for safety guardrailing ("No harassment; no sexual content; no instructions for weapons; response in a classroom-safe way.." etc.). All user inputs and chatbot responses are temporarily recorded on the back-end for a future teacher-specific review/ menu Learning Design Implications The structure of the Council Creator was influenced by PBLWorks , their research, and project examples. Suggested project phases, goals, and council roles are designed and prompted in a way to expose users to multiple depth-of-knowledge. (DOK) levels and Bloom's tiers. Some objectives will encourage students to research, synthesize, or gather first-hand resources. Others will encourage students to create artifacts to present to an audience, or engineer multi-disciplinary solutions. Responses are "chunked" and limited to prevent cognitive overload, to meet students at a developmentally appropriate level, and to provide achievable goals to promote self-efficacy and engagement. Metacognitive skills are exercised through reflective prompts for teachers and students. The Council Creator generates a pre-Launch set of reflective questions for teachers to examine biases, consider students' experience, and incorporate a wider community-level context. Future features may include student self- assessment rubrics and reflections on their responsible use of AI. Feasibility and Constaints The project is easily accessible to teachers on the internet. It will not be publicly available for use (as of now), as additional stress-testing and UX feedback is needed, and my personal APIs are connected to the projected. So a related constraint is the cost of the tool's use, as it utilizes LLMs at various stages. One option is to make the project publicly available on Github for users to connect their own APIs to, or for an organization, such as a school or district to use it with an organizational AI subscription. As of this writing, the tool has not been tested for mobile or tablet use, which could be a constraint for some audiences.

For K-12 audiences (I have options for Grade 3 and older currently), there are a number of considerations and concerns with students using AI tools such as chatbots. While I have attempted to structure the project to keep this audience in mind, it may not be feasible, or desirable to use the tool directly with younger students. A recommended path would be Grade 3-8 students to use with close guidance from an adult, such as students submitting their questions to the teacher, who then uses the tool. High School students would still need guidance and monitoring for the tool's appropriate use. Another feasibility consideration is the tool's practical use and learning curve for users, teachers and students alike. Mitigating this could involve significant UX testing and engineering, and revamping the UI for more guided use. I have begun exploring options (linked in my Figma presentation) for UI changes that are specific to different ages and education levels. The main question for users will be if this is a tool that is additive to their experience as a teacher or student. I believe it presents users with opportunities they could not access otherwise, and provides a structured, safe method for interactive with professionals and experts in a field. Learning Reflection There are two main strands of learning I experienced over the course of this project. The first is the technical knowledge that I acquired to launch such a project from idea to shipping a live, working product. I had some familiarity with aspects of how to achieve the task, but was able to incorporate learning from this course into existing technical skills I have practice over the last several years. Although I had used chatbots before, I had not prompted and built my own, or incorporated one into an existing or new project. Having to consider technical, pedagogical, moral/ethical, and philosophical issues during the project was a challenge, but worthwhile endeavor. I often reflected on design decisions and considered their efficacy, practicality, and pedagogical implications. There was not, and still is not, a clear answers on some of the thornier issues surrounding AI use, especially for younger audiences. I consider this aspect of the project to be a major takeaway and opportunity for future learning, especially as (A) innovative technology continues to drive forward and bring with it fraught societal issues and (B) public sentiment sways as the pressures from such technology proliferate. This will guide some of my thinking as I continue to develop learning products that use new technologies, from a personal, professional, and business standpoint. The answers may not ever be completely clear, but I look forward to continuing this learning process as I work toward creating memorable and effective experiences for learners!

Suggested Council Creator use (use second link at top of this document) 1. Upload an existing PBL project brief, such as one found at PBLWorks or any other document. 2. Review the suggested Essential Question and Learning Objectives. Edit, refine, and reorder. 3. Ask for Suggested project phases. Consider writing 1-2 phases manually and asking the AI for the rest. 4. Use Generate Council. Try the Regenerate button on one member and ask for a local expert for one member. Select which phases each member should be available for. 5. Click the Teacher Pre-Launch Reflection check box (Step 7) and review the reflective prompt. 6. Launch the Council! 7. Once in the council, try to replace one of the AI members with a human member (manually or with Search). 8. Click through the project phases and try using the prompt input to ask 1-2 council members a question at one time. 9. Check if local community resources are relevant to the project and your question. 10. Your council should be saved from the main site menu now, and you can even share the link with others (note: please don't share publicly, see Note below). Note: since this project is connected to my personal APIs, please limit prompting to 3-4 uses as multiple people may be reviewing this project at once. Thank you!

title: Mini-Design Challenge II  Prototyping an AI Council to Support PBL
pageTexts: Mini-Design Challenge II: Prototyping an AI Council to Support PBL Process Documentation Statement: My council roles are based on the different subject areas, learning objectives and phases of the project. Different members of the council will be available at different phases of the project. The workflow for the council interactions is as follows: • Phase 1: Cultural Ethnographer. Handoff: Once team completes the Community Chart, they are directed to proceed to Phase 2: Interstellar Linguist and Scientific Historian. Handoff: The linguist analyzes the draft list of artifacts to check for diversity of voices and prompts to consider how to present information to extraterrestrial entities. The Historian helps teams consider some of practical logistics of their choices, including choice of media and format, to ensure information is accessible many thousands of years into the future. > Phase 3: Logistics Architect. The logistics lead helps teams with the mathematical modeling involved in determining their storage limits. It can also encourage mathematics connections to other topics and provide support. > Phase 4: The Launch Visionary. The Visionary helps teams bring their vision together into a final product and can provide design and presentation guidance to the committee. As teams progress, they retain access to all previous members for consult, as they may need to refine or revise their project or plan. The teams will be given access to the AI Council after working on each phase, as well as 1-2 times during the phases. They will not have continuous access to the Council, but can submit specific questions via the teacher if they feel they need guidance and have hit a road block. To build my council, I create five separate personae on Google Gems that use Google Gemini. To create a simple UI, I used Cursor to build a web interface that puts each Gem on one screen with a prompt input. Because Gems cannot yet be embedded directly, or have multi-Gem capability on the same screen, the Gem's instructions are pasted into my web app's code, along with a Gemini API that uses Gemini Flash. As a result, the responses from the members are not as consistent and high quality as asking the Gems directly in the Google interface. To help with this, I added more detail into the context of the web app for each persona. This made up for some of the context that the Gems had within the Google interface (on Google platform, the Gems have access to a NotebookLM notebook I have that contains project documents and conversations about project planning).

To improve I would further tune each member persona. I have indirect ways for the members to communicate with each other - in the interface, after a response, a user has the option to send a response to another council member, and keep a running log of responses. I also need to refine responses to be more level-appropriate. Sometimes models give a deluge of information that is difficult for children to organize and process. Outline of my AI process for this stage: -Upload project information and background articles and documents in NotebookLM (PBL information, standards documents for ELA, math, science, and social studies, the Dorchester Project Brief as an example, and my Project Brief). -I asked for outlines of possible AI council members based on my description of the project and examples within the documents. I gave guidance to include information about possible standards to address and asked for explicit and implicit learning that could happen in different subject area. -I created the 5 council member personas in Google Gems, editing and adding onto the NotebookLM suggestions. -I asked Cursor for advice on how to integrate Google Gems into a simple web-based UI with a prompt input. Cursor described a method to manually enter persona instructions for each Gem, along with access to the project documents, and a Gemini API. -I tested the web UI and refined the UX and flow, adding options to save and pass on responses.

title: Mini-Design Challenge I  A Personalized Learning Experience with AI Chatbot
pageTexts: Mini-Design Challenge I: A Personalized Learning Experience with AI Chatbot My chatbot is named Curia. I am starting to think about how to integrate some version of it into a platform/ web-app I am developing for math students and educators. On my platform, there will not be text input available, but users will be able to "chat" with predetermined inputs (such as asking for help, answering about their grade level or experience, etc). I wanted to build a version to start thinking about how I want to prompt such a chatbot, even if the full version will not be embedded into my product. I used the prompts below, partially inspired by a recent report by Elevenlabs on best practices for structure prompts for agentic AI. I started with a short, broader prompt but was not getting the results I wanted. The chatbot was given far too much information without being asked. By expanding and providing a more detailed prompt, I was able to get results closer to my goals. I provided guidance for Curia to first ask about the user's level of understanding and adjust their prompts and level of challenge according to the user's grade level and familiarity with concepts (if they are an adult). I also provided guidance for how to support students or teachers with scaffolds and differentiated learning by asking follow- up questions and suggested strategies.
